stories.title: John Tanner: receiving, giving, and remembering
stories.introduction: John Tanner joined the Church in New York in 1832. Over the next eighteen years, his path led through Kirtland, Missouri, the Mississippi settlements, and the Salt Lake Valley. Along the way he gave money, endured violence and displacement, preached the gospel, and helped build two temples.

units.title: A hand offered in the name of Christ
paragraphs: John Tanner was a farmer and timberland owner in Bolton, New York, when missionaries brought him the restored gospel. He was fifty-four years old. Jared Carter recorded finding him unable to put weight on one foot after months of lameness. Tanner already believed in the Book of Mormon. Carter invited him to try walking in the name of Jesus Christ, took his hand, and commanded him to walk. In Carter’s account, Tanner was healed. Carter also recorded that Simeon was absent at that moment, praying separately for Tanner.

Tanner was baptized at Bolton Landing on September 17, 1832. The following February, Orson Pratt ordained him a priest. His new faith soon changed where he would live and what he would do with the property he had accumulated. The prosperous New York landowner began preparing to join the Saints in Ohio.

units.title: A decision that moved a household
paragraphs: In December 1834, Tanner felt an urgent need to go to Kirtland. He disposed of property and left with his household on Christmas morning. Their journey covered roughly five hundred miles; they arrived in January 1835.
Money was due on the temple land. Tanner lent Joseph Smith $2,000 to meet that need and received a note for the loan.

units.title: Resources put to work at Kirtland
paragraphs: Tanner advanced funds to the temple committee and helped back purchases of goods. His financial commitments put his resources at risk. He also became a stockholder in the Kirtland Safety Society.

The temple was a shared undertaking. The revelation now recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 109 preserves Joseph Smith’s dedication prayer, offered on March 27, 1836. It speaks of the Saints’ poverty, their work, and their desire to build a house to God’s name. Tanner’s contributions helped meet material needs within that larger effort of worship and sacrifice.

units.title: A family within the gathering and displacement
paragraphs: Tanner left Kirtland for Far West in 1838. In Missouri, he was severely beaten during the violence against the Saints. By the following spring he had moved again, this time to New Liberty in Illinois. In March 1840 he settled near Montrose, across the Mississippi River from Nauvoo.
He again helped with temple construction, contributing to the Nauvoo Temple while rebuilding his family’s life.

units.title: The note that became a remembered gift
paragraphs: According to the later family account, Tanner met Joseph Smith in Nauvoo before his 1844 mission and returned the $2,000 note. Joseph asked what to do with it. Tanner forgave the debt, making the loan an outright gift.

units.title: On the road again, 1844
paragraphs: In April 1844, Tanner left on a mission with David Pettegrew. Their journey took them by river to Pittsburgh, then on foot toward Buffalo. Pettegrew later reported walking 240 miles with Tanner and preaching along the way. From Buffalo they continued by boat toward Troy, carrying their message into New York and New England.

While they were still in the East, news reached them that Joseph and Hyrum Smith had been killed. Pettegrew’s December account describes their decision to visit acquaintances, bear testimony, and then turn westward. Tanner had left Nauvoo before the deaths; this was news received during his mission, far from Carthage.

sources.label: David Pettegrew’s December 1844 mission report — Times and Seasons

units.caption_boundary: Reconstruction of the journey described by Tanner’s companion; exact road, clothing and depicted moment unknown. No invented dialogue or news delivery.

units.title: A family journey to the valley
paragraphs: After leaving Nauvoo, Tanner reached the Council Bluffs area in 1846. Two years later he traveled with Elizabeth and other family members in the Willard Richards company. The company’s journey ran from July 3 to October 10, 1848. Tanner began it at sixty-nine and turned seventy along the way.

The family’s next home was South Cottonwood in the Salt Lake Valley. Tanner died there in 1850, aged seventy-one. His record had carried him from New York through Kirtland, Missouri, the Mississippi settlements, and finally Utah. The westward crossing was the last great move in that succession of homes.

stories.title: Eleazer Miller: a simple witness and a continuing life
stories.introduction: Eleazer Miller is remembered for the testimony that helped Brigham Young accept the restored gospel. His life also included early missions in the northeastern United States and Canada, a family journey across the plains, and many years in Utah.

units.title: A listener who wanted to know
paragraphs: Brigham Young encountered the Book of Mormon soon after its publication in 1830. Copies reached his family through the missionary work of Samuel Smith. Brigham examined the message for about two years before accepting baptism. He was a working craftsman in Mendon, New York, making and repairing furniture and fitting doors, windows, and other woodwork.

At home, his wife Miriam was ill with tuberculosis. Alongside earning a living, Brigham helped care for her and their two young daughters. His search for religious truth unfolded within those daily responsibilities. He read, listened, and considered what the missionaries taught before committing himself to the Church.

sources.label: The Ministry of Brigham Young

units.title: Before he became a missionary
paragraphs: Eleazer Miller was born in Coeymans, New York, in 1795, and married Rebecca Van Zant in 1816. The Church’s biographical database dates his baptism to May 1831, when he was thirty-five. Before he became the missionary remembered in Brigham Young’s conversion, he was himself a new convert.

His first recorded missions followed that same year, taking him into New York and Pennsylvania. In 1832 he would continue preaching in New York and cross into Upper Canada. The man who carried a testimony to other households had recently made his own commitment to the Church.

units.title: A missionary before the famous encounter
paragraphs: Miller carried his new faith beyond his own household. In the spring of 1832 he was thirty-six, and Brigham Young was thirty. Their paths met during this early period of missionary service in New York.

units.title: What Brigham remembered hearing
paragraphs: Brigham later described hearing a man who lacked polished speech or conspicuous learning bear a simple testimony of the Book of Mormon and Joseph Smith’s prophetic calling. Church teaching materials identify that missionary as Eleazer Miller. What stayed with Brigham was the conviction with which the witness was offered and the spiritual confirmation he himself experienced.

In his recollection, the Holy Ghost illuminated his understanding. He became convinced that the testimony was true. Miller’s words reached a man who had already spent a long time examining the gospel. The remembered encounter joins those two parts of Brigham’s conversion: patient inquiry and a personal witness of the Spirit.

units.title: An outward covenant in April 1832
paragraphs: On a cold, snowy day in April 1832, Miller baptized Brigham in Brigham’s own millstream. Brigham later remembered feeling humble and childlike, with an assurance that his sins were forgiven. He was confirmed and ordained an elder, and soon began preaching himself.

Miriam was baptized within a few weeks. Other members of the Young family and their neighbors also joined the growing Mendon branch. That September, Miriam died. Brigham’s first months in the Church held both the beginning of a new ministry and the loss of his wife, leaving him with their two daughters.

units.title: When the gathering outgrew the house
paragraphs: In 1832, Miller’s missionary work carried him into Upper Canada. A Church historical account places him at Ernesttown in June. A report he sent with fellow missionary Elial Strong describes people coming in such numbers that houses could not hold the meetings. They met in groves instead.

The missionaries also reported that hundreds were searching the scriptures. Some listeners were partly persuaded, while others had accepted their message. Their letter, dated March 19, 1833, recalled a field of work that had carried Miller beyond the communities of New York into gatherings under the trees of Upper Canada.

sources.label: Early Canadian missions — Church historical transcript
Miller and Strong’s report, discussed in The Brigham Young Family

units.caption_boundary: Grove teaching supported by missionaries’ report; exact grove, listeners and words unknown.

units.title: Three horses for the camp
paragraphs: On May 30, 1834, Miller joined the Camp of Israel, often called Zion’s Camp, east of Rochester. The history records his arrival with about half a dozen others and three horses. Several horses already with the camp were ailing, so the additional animals were welcome.

Two years after the baptisms in Mendon, Miller was again on the road with fellow believers. This time his arrival brought practical help to a traveling company. The history pauses to record the three horses because the camp needed animals able to continue the journey.

sources.label: History entry for May 30, 1834 — Joseph Smith Papers

units.caption_boundary: Reconstruction of documented arrival with three horses; no invented horse treatment, battle or named companion.

units.title: A life that continued westward
paragraphs: In 1848, Miller and Rebecca traveled west in Brigham Young’s company. Miller was fifty-two. John Heward, writing about his own journey, remembered starting west in company with Miller and spending several days at Winter Quarters before moving onward. Heward described the larger journey’s practical demands: finding feed, using buffalo chips for fuel, caring for footsore cattle, and receiving help with teams as the travelers approached the mountains.
The company reached the Salt Lake Valley in September. Miller and Rebecca had made the long journey from the settlements along the Missouri River to a new home in the West.

sources.label: Eleazer Miller — Church History Biographical Database

units.title: Ninety-five cents in the record
paragraphs: A small entry carries Miller’s story into life in Utah. The Great Salt Lake City Relief Society’s minutes for May 28, 1854 list a donation of ninety-five cents from “Elezor” Miller, identified in the published edition as Eleazer Miller. He was fifty-eight.

His gift appears among contributions of different amounts recorded by the society. Miller continued to live in Salt Lake City and died there on April 12, 1876, aged eighty. His surviving record reaches beyond his early missionary witness to the westward migration and a modest contribution to community relief.

stories.title: John Rowe Moyle: the stonecutter and the wooden leg
stories.introduction: John Rowe Moyle brought his family from England in 1856 and settled in Alpine, Utah. A skilled stonecutter, he traveled to Salt Lake City to work on the temple. After losing a leg, he fashioned a wooden replacement and eventually returned to the work.

units.title: A family on the road in 1856
paragraphs: John Rowe Moyle and his wife joined the Church in England in 1851. Five years later, they emigrated with their children. Moyle was forty-eight when the family joined Edmund Ellsworth’s handcart company for the overland journey to Utah.

The company reached Salt Lake City on September 26, 1856. Their overland journey was the final stage of a migration that had begun across the Atlantic. Before following Moyle into his work in Utah, we can return to his own account of that earlier crossing.

units.title: Before the plains: across the Atlantic
paragraphs: Before the handcarts came an ocean voyage. Moyle’s own journal records leaving Liverpool aboard the Samuel Curling on April 19, 1856. He and his family were bound for a new home far from England. At sea, storms rolled their luggage about and left beds wet.

They reached Boston on May 23. Three days later they continued by rail, arriving in Iowa on June 2. After about a week in camp, they set out with Ellsworth’s first handcart company. The ocean crossing, the railway journey, and the preparations in Iowa brought them to the beginning of the long walk across the plains.

sources.label: John Rowe Moyle’s journal — Saints by Sea

units.caption_boundary: Interpretive1856 emigrant voyage based on Moyle’s journal; exact deck and pictured moment unknown.

units.title: A skill offered to a shared undertaking
paragraphs: The Moyles settled in Alpine, south of Salt Lake City. Their home and farm were there, while the temple site lay about twenty-two miles away. Moyle was an accomplished stonecutter, and his skill was wanted for the temple. He undertook the journey on foot, leaving the family’s horse available for work at home.
His stone house survives at the historic Moyle property, now an Alpine city park. The home preserves the setting of the family life and farm work that continued alongside his temple service.

units.title: The distance between home and the work
paragraphs: The weekly journey began before daylight. In the account retold by Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Moyle left home at about two o’clock on Monday morning to reach work by eight. He stayed in Salt Lake City during the week. After work ended on Friday evening, he walked home again, arriving around midnight.
During those working weeks he lodged with a son in Salt Lake City. Friday’s return took him back to the farm and family in Alpine; Monday brought the long outward journey again.

units.title: Making a way to walk again
paragraphs: An injury eventually cost Moyle a leg. During his recovery, he made a wooden replacement with an articulated ankle and foot. He practiced walking on it, gradually rebuilding the endurance needed for the journey to Salt Lake City. Uchtdorf’s account describes pain and persistence as he learned to use it.
The Ensign Peak Foundation’s site history reports that Moyle’s wooden leg is displayed at the Daughters of Utah Pioneers Museum in Salt Lake City.

units.title: Remembering the worker beyond the obstacle
paragraphs: Moyle returned to temple work. Learning to walk with the wooden leg enabled him to take up the journeys and skilled labor that had filled his working weeks. The story remembered his persistence through the loss of a leg and his effort to keep serving.

units.title: Holiness to the Lord
paragraphs: The words associated with Moyle’s most remembered work are “Holiness to the Lord.” A later account supplied by his family describes him climbing scaffolding on the east side of the Salt Lake Temple to carve the inscription. His work gave lasting expression to the purpose of the building he had helped construct.

The inscription remains part of the temple. An official 2025 restoration report credits Moyle and describes renewed gilding of the panel on the east center tower. Moyle died on February 15, 1889, before the temple’s 1893 dedication. The words he carved outlasted him, still identifying the temple as a house of the Lord.
